definition:
Worship is the whole response of God's people to who God is and what he has done. In Scripture it includes bowing before him, serving him, offering sacrifice, keeping his festivals, singing and praying, hearing his word, and sharing the meals he gives, and in the New Testament it widens to include the offering of one's whole life. Its measure is not first its form but its object and its obedience: worship is owed to the true God alone, it answers his own revelation of himself, and it cannot be separated from how the worshiper treats his neighbor. The English word goes back to an Old English term for ‘worthiness’, but the Bible's own vocabulary is more concrete.

The most common Hebrew word is hishtachavah, ‘to bow down’ or ‘prostrate oneself’, used about 170 times, whether before God, before a king, or before an idol. Older grammars treated it as a form of the verb shachah; since the discovery of Ugaritic texts many scholars parse it instead as a rare stem of a root chawah, though the meaning is not in doubt. The second key word is avad, ‘to work’ or ‘to serve’, with its noun avodah, ‘work, service, worship’. The same word describes the harsh ‘service’ Israel gave Pharaoh (Exodus 1:14) and the service God demands when he says, “let My son go so that he may worship Me” (Exodus 4:23), so that the exodus is a transfer from one service to another. Israel's worship also speaks with halal, ‘to praise’ (the root of hallelujah), barak, ‘to bless’, and yadah, ‘to give thanks’ or ‘confess’. The Greek New Testament uses proskyneō, ‘to bow down, do obeisance’, the usual translation of hishtachavah, about sixty times; latreuō and latreia, ‘to serve’ and ‘service’, always of religious service; and leitourgeō, ‘to perform a public service’, from which the word liturgy comes.
ot:
Worship begins at the edges of Genesis. Some interpreters, following Gordon Wenham's 1986 essay on sanctuary symbolism in the garden of Eden, note that the man was placed in Eden “to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15), using the pair of verbs later used together of the Levites who keep and serve at the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7-8), and read Eden as the first sanctuary. The first recorded offerings, Cain's and Abel's, already show that God weighs the worshiper as well as the gift: “the LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering, but He had no regard for Cain and his offering” (Genesis 4:4-5), and Hebrews later says Abel offered “by faith” (Hebrews 11:4). “At that time men began to call upon the name of the LORD” (Genesis 4:26). The patriarchs build altars where God appears to them (Genesis 12:7-8), and Abraham tells his servants on the way to Moriah, “The boy and I will go over there to worship” (Genesis 22:5), worship that turns out to mean offering what he loves most.

In Exodus, worship is the goal of redemption. God tells Moses that the sign of his mission will be that “all of you will worship God on this mountain” (Exodus 3:12). At Sinai the covenant is sealed with a meal in God's presence, when the elders “saw the God of Israel” and “they ate and drank” (Exodus 24:10-11). God then gives the tabernacle, “so that I may dwell among them,” to be built “according to the pattern I show you” (Exodus 25:8-9). The next scene shows how easily worship goes wrong. With the golden calf, Aaron proclaims “a feast to the LORD” (Exodus 32:5): the people have not simply turned to another god but have tried to worship the LORD in a form he forbade. Leviticus sets out the sacrifices (the burnt, grain, peace, purification, and guilt offerings), the priesthood, and the calendar of appointed feasts (Leviticus 23), from Passover to the Day of Atonement and Booths. It also records the death of Aaron's sons, who “offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, contrary to His command” (Leviticus 10:1), with God's word: “To those who come near Me I will show My holiness” (Leviticus 10:3). Deuteronomy gathers Israel's sacrifices to “the place the LORD your God will choose” (Deuteronomy 12:5) and warns, “See that you do everything I command you; do not add to it or subtract from it” (Deuteronomy 12:32). Under all the ritual stands the heart: “you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:5).

The Psalms are Israel's worship in words, gathered over centuries and used in the second temple as a book of praise and prayer. Chronicles credits David with organizing Levitical singers and musicians, the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, “to prophesy with the accompaniment of lyres, harps, and cymbals” (1 Chronicles 25:1). The Psalms call the whole earth to praise: “O come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD our Maker” (Psalm 95:6), and “Serve the LORD with gladness; come into His presence with joyful songs” (Psalm 100:2). They include thanksgiving, confession, and lament as well as praise, and they already look past the altar: “May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering” (Psalm 141:2). God does not need what is offered, “for the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof” (Psalm 50:12), and what he wants most is a contrite heart: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit” (Psalm 51:17). Isaiah's call begins in the temple with the seraphim crying, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory” (Isaiah 6:3), and the prophet's first response is confession.

The prophets judged Israel's worship by its obedience. Samuel told Saul that “obedience is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22). In the eighth century BC Amos heard God say, “I hate, I despise your feasts,” and “let justice roll on like a river” (Amos 5:21, 24); Isaiah called Judah's offerings worthless while its hands were “covered with blood” (Isaiah 1:15); Hosea spoke for a God who desires “mercy, not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6); and Micah answered the question of what to bring with “act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). Jeremiah warned against trusting in the chant ‘This is the temple of the LORD’ (Jeremiah 7:4). Nineteenth-century critics sometimes read these texts as rejecting ritual altogether; most interpreters now read them as condemning ritual cut off from justice and covenant loyalty, since the same prophets expected a purified temple. Isaiah named the root problem: “These people draw near to Me with their mouths and honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me” (Isaiah 29:13). The exile, with the temple destroyed in 587 or 586 BC, forced Israel to worship without altar or sacrifice, and prayer, the reading of Scripture, and the gatherings that became the synagogue took a central place. Hosea had already spoken of offering “the fruit of our lips” (Hosea 14:2), and Malachi foresaw that “In every place, incense and pure offerings will be presented in My name” among the nations (Malachi 1:11).
nt:
In the Gospels people bow before Jesus: the magi “fell down and worshiped Him” (Matthew 2:11), the disciples in the boat “worshiped Him, saying, ‘Truly You are the Son of God!’” (Matthew 14:33), and the women at the empty tomb “grasped His feet, and worshiped Him” (Matthew 28:9). Yet Jesus insists that worship belongs to God alone, answering Satan from Deuteronomy, “Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only” (Matthew 4:10). He accepts what he says is due only to God, which is part of the New Testament's witness to his deity. Scholars such as Larry Hurtado (Lord Jesus Christ, 2003) and Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the God of Israel, 2008) have argued that this devotion to Jesus alongside God, within a strictly monotheistic Judaism, appears from the earliest Christian sources. Jesus himself worshiped in the synagogue “As was His custom” (Luke 4:16) and at the temple feasts, but he also spoke of “the temple of His body” (John 2:21). To the Samaritan woman, who asked whether worship belonged on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem, he answered that “the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth” (John 4:23). Interpreters differ over whether ‘spirit’ here means the Holy Spirit or the inner person and whether ‘truth’ means sincerity or the reality now revealed in Jesus; many hold both senses together. What is clear is that the place of worship is no longer a mountain but a person. Jesus also repeated Isaiah's charge against lip-service, adding, “They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men” (Matthew 15:9).

The first Christians kept meeting in the temple courts and in homes. “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer” (Acts 2:42), a summary that names the main parts of Christian gatherings ever since. They met “On the first day of the week” to break bread (Acts 20:7), and John received his vision “On the Lord’s day” (Revelation 1:10). The church at Antioch was “worshiping the Lord and fasting” (Acts 13:2) when the Spirit sent Barnabas and Saul, the verb there being leitourgeō. Paul describes gatherings where “everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation,” all for building up the church and done “in a proper and orderly manner” (1 Corinthians 14:26, 40). He tells Timothy to devote himself “to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching” (1 Timothy 4:13), and he tells the churches to sing “psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs” (Colossians 3:16, Ephesians 5:19). Many scholars think passages such as Philippians 2:6-11 and Colossians 1:15-20 preserve early Christian hymns or confessions. In Philippians the words of Isaiah 45:23, where every knee bows to the LORD, are applied to Jesus: “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10). The Lord's Supper, which proclaims “the Lord’s death until He comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26), is treated in the study on the sacraments.

The sacrifices of the old covenant are fulfilled in Christ, who “offered for all time one sacrifice for sins” (Hebrews 10:12), and so the language of sacrifice passes to the whole life of the believer. Paul urges believers “to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship” (Romans 12:1). The Greek phrase logikē latreia is translated ‘spiritual’, ‘reasonable’, or ‘rational’ worship; it describes service that fits what God has done and engages the renewed mind. Hebrews names two sacrifices that remain: “a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name,” and doing good and sharing, “for with such sacrifices God is pleased” (Hebrews 13:15-16). James defines pure religion as caring “for orphans and widows in their distress” (James 1:27). Gathered worship is not abolished by this wider sense. Hebrews invites believers to “draw near” through Jesus their priest and warns against neglecting to meet together (Hebrews 10:22-25), and it describes the gathered church as having come “to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” and to “myriads of angels in joyful assembly” (Hebrews 12:22-23), so that it is to worship “with reverence and awe” (Hebrews 12:28).

Revelation opens heaven's worship. The living creatures cry “Holy, Holy, Holy,” echoing Isaiah 6, and the elders praise God as Creator: “Worthy are You, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things” (Revelation 4:11). Then the same worship is given to the Lamb as Redeemer: “Worthy are You to take the scroll and open its seals, because You were slain” (Revelation 5:9), until every creature says, “To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever” (Revelation 5:13). A multitude “from every nation and tribe and people and tongue” stands before the throne (Revelation 7:9). When John falls at the feet of the angel, he is told twice, “Worship God” (Revelation 19:10, 22:9). The city at the end has no temple, “because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple” (Revelation 21:22), and there “His servants will worship Him” (Revelation 22:3).

keyTexts.why: The first offerings show that God regards the worshiper as well as the gift, a theme Hebrews 11:4 explains as the difference faith makes.
The goal of the exodus is that Israel will worship God at his mountain; redemption is for worship.
The golden calf is worship offered to the LORD in a form he forbade, the Bible's first great warning that sincerity does not make worship acceptable.
Nadab and Abihu's unauthorized fire shows the holiness of the God who is approached and the seriousness of approaching him on his terms.
The Shema grounds all worship in the one LORD and in love with the whole heart, soul, and strength.
A call to sing, bow, and kneel before the LORD as King and Maker, followed by a warning to hear his voice today.
Isaiah's vision joins worship, holiness, and confession: the prophet who sees the King first sees his own uncleanness.
God rejects feasts and songs offered by a people who deny justice, the sharpest prophetic word that worship and ethics cannot be separated.
In place of ever larger offerings God asks for justice, mercy, and a humble walk with him.
Jesus relocates worship from a sacred mountain to himself and the Spirit, calling for worship in spirit and truth.
The first church gives itself to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer, in the temple courts and in homes.
Worship becomes the offering of the whole bodily life to God, answered by the renewing of the mind.
The gathered church has come to the heavenly Jerusalem and is called to worship with reverence and awe before a consuming fire.
After Christ's sacrifice, the offerings that remain are praise from the lips and doing good to others.
Heaven's worship honors God as Creator and the slain Lamb as Redeemer, and draws every creature into it.

history:
The earliest descriptions of Christian worship come from both sides of the church door. The Roman governor Pliny the Younger, writing to the emperor Trajan around 112 (Letters 10.96), reported that Christians met before dawn on a fixed day, sang a hymn to Christ as to a god, and bound themselves by oath not to commit crimes, then later met again for an ordinary meal. The Didache, a church manual from the late first or early second century, gives prayers for the Eucharist, tells believers to gather on the Lord's day and confess their sins, and applies Malachi 1:11 to that offering. Justin Martyr's First Apology (about 155, chapter 67) describes a Sunday service in Rome: the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read as long as time allows, the presider exhorts, the people stand to pray, bread and wine are brought and blessed with thanksgiving, the people answer Amen, deacons carry the elements to the absent, and a collection is taken for widows, orphans, and the needy. A church order called the Apostolic Tradition, traditionally attributed to Hippolytus of Rome and dated around 215 (both attribution and date are now widely disputed), contains an early eucharistic prayer with the opening call to lift up the heart. After Constantine made Sunday a day of rest in 321, public worship grew more elaborate; the pilgrim Egeria described the services of Jerusalem in the 380s, and the Eastern churches developed the liturgies still used under the names of Basil and John Chrysostom. Benedict's Rule, written in the sixth century, organized monastic life around daily hours of prayer in which the whole Psalter was sung each week.

The iconoclast controversy tested the line between worship and honor. From the 720s Byzantine emperors ordered the removal of religious images, and the Second Council of Nicaea (787) restored them, distinguishing latreia, the worship due to God alone, from the veneration shown to icons, and teaching, with Basil of Caesarea, that honor given to an image passes to the one it depicts. Icons were finally restored in the East in 843. Medieval Western worship centered on the Latin Mass and the daily office. The Reformation reshaped worship around the vernacular, the preached word, congregational song, and a simplified Supper. Luther revised the Mass in his Formula Missae (1523) and German Mass (1526) and wrote hymns for congregations to sing; Zurich under Zwingli removed images from its churches in 1524 and silenced music in worship; Calvin's Geneva sang metrical psalms, gathered in the Genevan Psalter completed in 1562; Thomas Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer (1549, revised 1552 and 1662) gave English worship its shape. The Council of Trent led to the Roman Missal of 1570 under Pius V. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, questions 96 to 98) forbade images of God and their use in teaching, and the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 21) stated the regulative principle, that God may be worshiped only in the way he has appointed in Scripture, while the Westminster Directory for Public Worship (1645) replaced the prayer book in Presbyterian churches.

Later centuries added new streams. Isaac Watts's Hymns and Spiritual Songs (1707) helped move English-speaking Protestants from metrical psalms to hymns, and Charles Wesley wrote thousands of hymns for the Methodist revival. The Quakers, from the 1650s, gathered in silence to wait on the Spirit. American revivalism in the nineteenth century, including Charles Finney's ‘new measures’ in the 1820s and 1830s, shaped worship toward decision and response, and the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles from 1906 gave rise to Pentecostal worship with its expectation of spiritual gifts. The Second Vatican Council's constitution on the liturgy, Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963), called for the full, conscious, and active participation of the people and opened the way to worship in the vernacular. In the late twentieth century, contemporary worship music, much of it rooted in the Jesus movement and charismatic renewal of the 1960s and 1970s, spread across denominations and set off long arguments over style that are sometimes called the worship wars. The principle often summarized in the Latin phrase lex orandi, lex credendi (the rule of prayer is the rule of belief), traced to Prosper of Aquitaine in the fifth century, names what every tradition has found: the way a church worships shapes what it believes.

differ.body: Presbyterian and Reformed churches, following the Westminster Confession, hold that in public worship the church may do only what God has commanded in Scripture, whether expressly or by good and necessary consequence: reading and preaching the word, prayer, singing, the sacraments, and a few other elements. Its defenders point to Nadab and Abihu, to the golden calf, to Deuteronomy 12:32, and to Jesus' rebuke of worship built on human precepts. They argue that the principle protects both God's honor and the conscience of worshipers, who should never be bound to practices God did not require. Some within this tradition sing only the psalms, without instruments, while most apply the principle more broadly.

Lutheran and Anglican churches, and many other Protestants, hold that the church may use in worship whatever Scripture does not forbid, as long as it agrees with the gospel and builds up the church. The Augsburg Confession (1530, article 15) keeps rites that can be observed without sin, and the Thirty-Nine Articles allow each church to order its ceremonies for edification. Defenders note that Scripture gives few detailed rules for Christian gatherings, that Jesus took part in synagogue services and the Feast of Dedication (John 10:22), neither of which the law of Moses commanded, and that Paul's standard for worship is edification and good order (1 Corinthians 14:26, 40).

Eastern Orthodox, Roman Catholic, and many Anglican and Lutheran Christians understand the church's worship as a participation in the worship of heaven described in Hebrews 12 and Revelation 4-5, centered on the Eucharist and ordered by a liturgy received from the ancient church. They argue that fixed forms carry the whole faith, guard it from the preferences of each generation, and teach believers to pray with Scripture, since most of a historic liturgy is scriptural language. The church year, which retells the life of Christ from Advent to Pentecost, is valued as a way of living inside the gospel story.

Many Baptist, free-church, Pentecostal, and charismatic Christians prefer simple forms and freedom for the Spirit to lead. They point to the open participation of 1 Corinthians 14:26, where each believer may bring a song, a teaching, or a gift, and to the Psalms' call to lift hands, clap, shout, and dance before the LORD. They value spontaneous prayer, extended congregational singing, and the expectation that God will act in the gathering, while insisting, with Paul, that everything be done in order and for building up the body.

errors:
Scripture's first test of worship is its object. Giving to any creature the trust, love, and worship that belong to God alone is idolatry, whether the creature is a carved image, an angel (Colossians 2:18, Revelation 19:10), a nation, or money. The fourth-century church saw the reverse side of this truth: because Christians had always worshiped Christ, Athanasius argued that the Arian teaching that the Son is a creature would make that worship idolatrous. All traditions reject worship of saints, angels, or images as if they were God; Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold that their distinction between worship and veneration keeps that line, while most Protestants believe the practice of venerating saints and icons blurs it. The golden calf shows a second error, worshiping the true God in a form of one's own devising, as though sincerity made any worship acceptable.

The prophets and Jesus exposed a third error, worship with the lips while the heart is far away and the neighbor is oppressed. Worship that ignores justice, that treats ritual as a way to manage God, or that assumes God needs what is offered (Psalm 50:12) is rejected throughout Scripture. The opposite errors appear too: reducing worship to private feeling and neglecting the gathered church (Hebrews 10:25), or turning the gathering into a performance judged by how it makes the worshiper feel. Worship aimed at securing prosperity or success treats God as a means rather than the end, which is the heart of idolatry in a religious form.
life:
Because worship is the whole response to God, it is not confined to an hour on Sunday, yet it is not less than that hour. The gathered church hears God's word, prays, sings, confesses its faith, and shares the Lord's Supper, and these practices train the heart for the worship of ordinary life: work done honestly, money shared, enemies forgiven, the body offered to God rather than to appetite. Paul's ‘living sacrifice’ means that the kitchen, the office, and the hospital room are places of service to God as truly as the sanctuary.

Worship also forms the worshiper. The psalmist warns that those who trust idols become like them, and the New Testament promises that those who behold the Lord's glory are changed into his image. What a person praises, fears, and loves most will shape who that person becomes. Worship begins with God's worth rather than with the worshiper's mood, so the Psalms give words for joy and for grief, for praise and for lament, and the hope of Revelation is a gathering from every nation that finally worships without distraction or sin.
questions: The prophets condemned worship that was careful about ritual but careless about justice. Where might our worship be tempted to separate the two?
Romans 12:1 calls the offering of the whole body worship. What would it change to think of your daily work as service offered to God?
The regulative, normative, liturgical, and free-church traditions each guard something. What does each one protect, and what might each learn from the others?
